etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English lyme, lym, lime, from Old English līm, from Proto-West Germanic *līm, from Proto-Germanic *līmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂leyH- (“to smear”).

Cognate with Saterland Frisian Liem (“glue”), Dutch lijm, German Leim (“glue”), Danish lim (from Old Norse lím), Latin limus (“mud”).

definitions.definition: (chemistry) Any inorganic material containing calcium, usually calcium oxide (quicklime) or calcium hydroxide (slaked lime).

quote.citation: 1952, L.F. Salzman, Building in England, page 149:
quote.text: Lime, which is the product of the burning of chalk or limestone, might be bought ready burnt, or it could be burnt in kilns specially constructed in the neighbourhood of the building operations.

definitions.definition: (poetic) Any gluey or adhesive substance; something which traps or captures someone; sometimes a synonym for birdlime.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: Monster, come, put some lime upon your fingers, and away with the rest.

quote.citation: 1835, William Wordsworth, They called Thee Merry England, in old time [first line of unnamed poem]:
quote.text: Like the lime which foolish birds are caught with.

quote.citation: 1980, Peter Evans, Peter Sellers: The Mask Behind the Mask, page 30:
quote.text: Sellers moved on until he was actually trusted to operate the limes, the spotlights that can make or destroy an artist's act.

quote.citation: 2018, Robert Charles Hines, Twists and Turns: 13 Tales of the Uneasy, page 121:
quote.text: Then out of the blue, a spotlight much like the “limes” in a theatre, lit up what seemed like a Punch and Judy tent  […]  He struggled even more, when from out of the shadows and into the bright light of the limes, stepped Uncle Jolly.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To treat with calcium hydroxide or calcium oxide (lime).

quote.text: If I were you, I'd lime.

quote.citation: 1598–1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “Much Adoe about Nothing”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i]:
quote.text: URSULA. She's lim'd, I warrant you: we have caught her, madam.HERO. If it prove so, then loving goes by haps:Some Cupid kills with arrows, some with traps.

quote.citation: 1891, Thomas Hardy, Tess of the d'Urbervilles, volume 1, London: James R. Osgood, McIlvaine and Co., page 39:
quote.text: Abraham, like his parents, seemed to have been limed and caught by the ensnaring inn.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Lime (17th c.) and line (16th c.) are alterations of obsolete lind, from Middle English lynde, from Old English lind, from Proto-Germanic *lindijō. The phonetic development is unusual, but it has been suggested that it began in compounds (loss of -d- perhaps before tree, the change to -m- before labials as in bark or wood). Doublet of linden, which see.

definitions.definition: A deciduous tree of the genus Tilia, especially Tilia × europaea; the linden tree.

quote.citation: 1828, Thomas Keightley, The Fairy Mythology, volume I, London: William Harrison Ainsworth, page 158:
quote.text: The linden or lime tree is the favourite haunt of the Elves and cognate beings; and it is not safe to be near it after sunset.

quote.citation: 1871, George Eliot [pseudonym; Mary Ann Evans], chapter III, in Middlemarch […], volume I, Edinburgh, London: William Blackwood and Sons, →OCLC, book I, page 38:
quote.text: But there was nothing of an ascetic's expression in her bright full eyes, as she looked before her, not consciously seeing, but absorbing into the intensity of her mood, the solemn glory of the afternoon with its long swathes of light between the far-off rows of limes, whose shadows touched each other.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French lime, from Spanish lima, from Arabic لِيمَة (līma), from Persian لیمو (limu). Doublet of lemon.

definitions.definition: Any of several green citrus fruit, somewhat smaller and sharper-tasting than a lemon.
Any of the trees that bear limes, especially Key lime, Citrus aurantiifolia.
(uncountable) A brilliant, sometimes yellowish, green colour associated with the fruits of a lime tree.
(fandom slang) A fan fiction story which contains sexual references, but stops short of full, explicit descriptions of sexual activity (coined by analogy with lemon).

quote.citation: 1998 June 8, Gary Kleppe, “[Ranma][Fanfic] Tangled Web”, in rec.arts.anime.creative‎[1] (Usenet):
quote.text: WARNING: This is a lime. While it does not show explicit sex, as a lemon would, references to sexual situations abound.

quote.citation: 1998 December 29, jiml...@earthlink.net, “[EVA][FanFic][Lemon]  Garden of EVA 0:6x - Wet Dreams Bite!”, in rec.arts.anime.creative‎[2] (Usenet):
quote.text: Even with all the sex in Garden of EVA, I still think the main stories are better for just being the lemon-scented limes that they are.

quote.citation: 2001 November 27, Schemer, “[Ranma/SF][FanFic] A Learning Experience - Chapter 01”, in rec.arts.anime.creative‎[3] (Usenet):
quote.text: I have no intention of writing any lemon scenes, limes are possibilities but unlikely and if they occur they will be few in number.

definitions.definition: Having the aroma or flavor of lime.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Either a back-formation of limer or from the derogatory term limey, a term first given to British soldiers but also used by Trinidadians for American soldiers who used to hang out idle in Port of Spain during World War 2.

definitions.definition: (Caribbean, Barbados, Trinidad and Tobago, informal) To hang out or socialize in an informal, relaxed environment, especially with friends, for example at a party or on the beach.
(Caribbean, Trinidad & Tobago) A casual gathering to socialize.
